title: migrateMint inflates id-6 supply with zero on-chain assertion that NFTStakerV2 reward runway has been topped up — early migrators can permanently dilute existing id-6 stakers' yield if deployment ordering is off
description:
Each call to migrateMint increases `_totalSupply[6]` by `amount` without any corresponding economic backing on the dispatcher side (no USDS paid, no sUSDS wrapped, no BPT or phUSD-equivalent added). The protocol's claim that 'migrations preserve economic value' relies on a separate, deployment-time owner action (per migration plan step 11): minting fresh phUSD into NFTStakerV2 to give the new staker the same forward runway-in-seconds the old staker has. That mint is explicitly a *separate broadcast* from the migration deployment ('that broadcast does not require the phUSD-minter role and can be reviewed independently').

If the broadcast order is reversed — migrations open before the staker is funded — early migrators stake their freshly minted id-6 NFTs into an underfunded staker and (per the staker's accrual math, typically `(amount * accRewardPerShare) / ACC_PRECISION - rewardDebt`) earn rewards calibrated against an `accRewardPerShare` that has not yet absorbed the runway-top-up. When the top-up arrives, it elevates `accRewardPerShare` for all current stakers, including the early migrators who already 'paid' their rewardDebt at the lower share. This is the classic 'snapshot-stake-before-distribution' MEV in MasterChef-style stakers.

The magnitude is bounded by the size of the top-up relative to the existing TVL, but for a migration sized to ~139 NFTs and 910 phUSD of inherited runway plus a fresh top-up, the divergence between (early-migrator share) and (delayed-migrator share) can be material to the migration's intended economic neutrality.

migrateMint provides no on-chain assertion that:
  - The new staker exists at the moment of migration.
  - The new staker holds the configured runway.
  - The migration window has opened per the deployment script's intent.

Consequence: a strict reading of the migration plan suggests the team intends migrations to be economically neutral — but the on-chain code does not enforce this. The neutrality depends entirely on operational discipline (broadcast ordering, top-up timing).
exploit_path:
Setup: migration plan step ordering misexecuted. Migration broadcast deploys (4)-(10) successfully, but step 11 (phUSD top-up of new staker) is delayed by N hours due to (a) cold-wallet signer unavailable, (b) governance friction, (c) operator awaiting market conditions.

Exploit:
1. Bot watching mempool sees BalancerPoolerV3 installed and authorised.
2. Bot already holds id-4 NFTs (or buys them OTC from forgotten old-staker holders).
3. Bot calls `migrateMint(N, bot)` and immediately `staker.stakeFor(bot, N)` (or stakes directly).
4. Time T+1h: top-up lands. `accRewardPerShare` jumps. Bot's stake share captures a proportional slice.
5. Bot has captured runway that, per the migration plan's intent, should have been distributed across all id-6 stakers including those who staked before migration opened.

Magnitude bound: bot's stake fraction × the marginal runway-top-up. If pre-migration existing id-6 stakers hold 100 NFTs and the bot adds 41 migrated NFTs against a 910 phUSD top-up plus matched fresh mint, the bot captures ~30% of the top-up (~273 phUSD) for the migration's economic transfer it was meant to neutrally provide.

Note: This finding is NOT about NFTStakerV2's math being wrong — that's an out-of-scope submodule. It's about migrateMint providing zero on-chain coupling to the downstream staker's funding state. The function inflates supply with no atomic check on solvency.
mainnet_realism: Migration plan step 11 is explicitly 'a separate owner-signed call'. Multi-stage broadcasts with phUSD-minter-role separation are operationally common — the plan even calls out the role separation as a feature, not a defect. Manual top-up ordering is a known operational hazard for MasterChef-style stakers; documented MEV patterns exist for snapshot-stake-before-distribution on Synthetix, Curve gauges, and others. Realism for an opportunistic id-4 holder watching the deployment broadcast: high.
recommendation:
Three options, increasingly invasive:
(a) Add a `migrationOpen` boolean to BalancerPoolerV2, owner-settable, defaulting to FALSE at deploy. The owner sets it TRUE only after step 11 of the deployment plan completes (staker funded). migrateMint reverts when migrationOpen is false. Cheap, clean, matches the plan's 'one-shot' framing.
(b) Inject the new NFTStakerV2 address as an immutable in migrateMint's deployment, and require the staker's `rewardBudget` (or equivalent solvency view) to exceed a configured threshold before each migration. More invasive and couples this contract to an out-of-scope submodule.
(c) Use a TWO-step migration: migrateMint flags the user as eligible (events / a mapping) but does not mint until the user calls `claimMigration()` in a second tx; the second tx checks the staker's solvency. Over-engineered for a one-shot migration.

Option (a) is recommended.
severity_rationale: Tentative Low (could promote to Medium if the team's deployment runbook does not include explicit ordering enforcement). The vulnerability requires (1) the deployment to ship migrations before staker top-up — a deviation from the plan — AND (2) an opportunistic actor in the mempool. The dilution is bounded by the bot's fraction of total id-6 stake, which for a fresh migration is modest. No direct theft; impact is value-leak from intended-recipients to opportunistic stakers. The plan is reviewable and reviewable-by-team, mitigating the operational risk. Per C4: 'state handling, function incorrect as to spec, issues with comments' applies to QA/Low. Promote to Medium ONLY if the team confirms the deployment broadcast cannot be ordered atomically (i.e., migrations MUST open before top-up due to the phUSD-minter role separation).
poc_notes: PoC requires NFTStakerV2 which is out-of-scope per user instruction. A scoped-down PoC could mock the staker accrual math (accRewardPerShare jump on top-up) and demonstrate the share-capture delta between early and late migrators. Recommend: defer PoC; flag for team review of deployment runbook.
